newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine tightens spending, steps up tax collection.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine tightens spending, steps up tax collection.

text.p: Ukraine will slap tight spending controls on state bodies and step up tax collection to stem a haemorrhaging of money from government coffers, the deputy prime minister for the economy said on Thursday.

Viktor Pynzenyk told a news conference that the controls -- to be implemented starting this month after a February presidential decree -- were needed to adhere to the as-yet unapproved budget and push through economic reforms.

"Budget discipline cannot be achieved solely through the tax reform package being reviewed by parliament," he said, referring to a recent presidential decree on strengthening budget discipline and tightening controls.

The decree limits further spending until the 1997 budget is passed, calls for a law holding state enterprise managers and officials criminally liable for overspending and calls for the immediate creation of tax collection services.

Parliament, dominated by conservative deputies, is far past its January deadline to approve the budget and the tax reform package underpinning it, leaving government bodies and enterprises free to spend money as they wish.

Pynzenyk, regarded as a keen reformer, said the government might have to dip into central bank reserves, estimated at about $3.3 billion, to make ends meet until the budget is passed this month or next.
"We cannot sit with our hands folded and do nothing about those who are not paying taxes not because they cannot pay but because they do not want to pay," he said.
Economic reform in this former Soviet republic of 52 million people has been slow and tax evasion is widespread, with 50 percent of the economy a grey market, or shadow, economy.
The 1997 budget and various reforms must be approved before Ukraine can receive a new $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility credit from the International Monetary Fund.
A system in which firms can legally avoid paying taxes by officially declaring they have no funds drags down the economy.
Pynzenyk has come down hard on government officials and corruption, saying some officials are pocketing workers' wages and that salary arrears are about $1.4 billion.
"They get the money but they don't pay workers," he said.

"Is it normal when the manager of a government firm does not pay its people but drives up to the government in a $150,000 car? This is happening with government enterprises and we have not had the laws to stop this."
The decree on spending controls orders courts to speed up bankruptcy hearings and to process tax evasion cases faster.
It also orders the government to devise a plan to pay off loans taken on by enterprises which were guaranteed by the Ukrainian government.
